notes.title: The 40M finale: change one variable
content: Seven phases in, Aizen sat at 48–52% with a see-saw problem: every fix to one category cost another. Phase 8 changed exactly one thing — size. 8 layers / 384 dim / 6 heads became 12 / 512 / 8, about 40M parameters. Same tokenizer, same 512 context, same warm-up-and-cosine recipe.

Before training I caught two bugs that had been quietly wrecking earlier runs: a per-chunk reseeding flaw that shrank every resumed run, and silent Metal GPU memory corruption above batch size ~20. Neither threw an error. Both were found by checking numbers that should have matched and didn’t.

Result: 60.75% — every category at an all-time high, and the see-saw stopped. Because only one variable moved, the result is believable: the gain is the capacity, not a lucky recipe. And 40M sits inside the 30–50M cap I set on day one.

notes.title: Proportion matters as much as presence
content: Phase 6 added real public data for the first time — bAbI reading and deduction tasks — next to my synthetic patterns and 3-digit arithmetic. First attempt: 47.25%, up only two points, with reading comprehension actually falling. The bAbI slice had swamped everything else.

Capping bAbI at 2,400 examples and re-running lifted it to 52.25%. Same sources, different dosage, five-point swing. Phase 7 taught the mirror lesson: adding conversation memory dipped the score to 48.0% — a deliberate trade for a capability the benchmark doesn’t measure.
So two rules I now train by: the ratio of a dataset matters as much as whether it is present, and not every worthwhile step is a benchmark step.

notes.title: Measure before you improve
content: Before touching Aizen's training, I built the measuring stick: a frozen set of 400 questions across 8 categories — arithmetic, multi-step, logic, patterns, general knowledge, instruction following, reading, coding — and an eval.py that scores any checkpoint the same way, every time.
Two rules made it work. The eval is frozen: I never tweak questions to make a model look better. And one training run per approved experiment: no quietly re-running until the number goes up.
The payoff was immediate. v0 scored 17% — an honest, slightly painful baseline. But every improvement after that was real, because the ruler never changed.

notes.title: Fine-tuning a tiny model is whack-a-mole
content: Phase 3 taught me that a 14M-parameter model has no spare capacity. Fine-tuning with an answer-masked loss (only the answer tokens count toward the loss) lifted the score from 17% to 26.5% — but categories moved against each other.
Fixing multi-step arithmetic hurt plain arithmetic. A targeted-fix dataset (Phase 3b) brought arithmetic back from 72 to 86 but dropped multi-step from 56 to 44. A see-saw.
Lesson: at this scale, every gradient step is a trade. You need per-category measurement to even see the trades you're making — a single overall number hides them.

notes.title: Writing a BPE tokenizer from scratch
content: Character-level models spend most of their capacity learning to spell. So I wrote byte-pair encoding from scratch — no libraries: count adjacent pairs, merge the most frequent, repeat to a 2048-token vocabulary.

Two design choices mattered more than the algorithm: digits stay single tokens (so arithmetic doesn't break on weird merges like '45' becoming one token), and newlines never merge (so the Q/A structure stays visible).
Retrained from scratch with the new tokenizer and a 512-token context, the same-size model jumped from 28.75% to 35.75%. Representation is leverage: identical parameters, better spent.

notes.title: Why pretraining matters even at 16M params
content: Aizen kept failing logic questions not because it couldn't reason, but because it couldn't read — it had only ever seen Q&A pairs, never flowing English.

So: 103MB of TinyStories, cleaned to ASCII, tokenized to 26.2M tokens with a 4096-vocab BPE, pretrained overnight for 16k steps as a plain language model. Then a short 2.5k-step masked-QA fine-tune on top.

Logic went from 12% to 66%. Overall: 35.75% → 45.25%. The pretrained model even writes coherent little stories. Comprehension comes from reading, not from flashcards — true for models, probably for people too.

notes.title: A language model is smaller than you think
content: The whole of Aizen — attention, MLP blocks, embeddings, the training loop — is a handful of readable Python files. No framework magic: model.py defines the Transformer, a training script feeds it batches, a checkpoint file carries weights, vocab and config together.
Building it demystified every buzzword. 'Attention' is a few matrix multiplications. 'Context length' is an array size. 'Training' is a loop that nudges numbers.
If you can write Python and have a laptop, you can build a language model. It won't be GPT — mine is charmingly wrong about 63 + 26 sometimes — but you'll understand what GPT actually is.

notes.title: Building an OS-shaped portfolio
content: A portfolio is a claim about what you can build — so the site itself should be evidence. Gyan OS is a desktop: menu bar, dock with magnification, draggable windows with real z-ordering, apps.
The interesting engineering is state: a window manager is just a store mapping app ids to geometry plus a z-counter, and everything else is springs and pointer events.
Rule I kept from Aizen: no fake data. The benchmark numbers in the Aizen app are the real eval results, and the chat talks to the real model running on my machine — when it's offline, it says so.
